Modern software infrastructure accumulates what we term correctness debt: a class of defects that are not random bugs but structural properties of the deployment pipeline itself, properties that testing and monitoring rarely catch because the failure mode is either silent, pre-runtime, or masked by a layer that was supposed to prevent it. This paper synthesizes five specific findings from recent cs.SE, cs.PL, and cs.AR preprints into a candidate reading of why correctness debt is growing faster than the tools meant to address it. The thesis is a heuristic reading, not a derivation: the five mechanisms are analogous in structure but do not share a single formal framework, and the analogy could be falsified by showing the mechanisms are causally independent in practice. The five mechanisms are: (1) type systems that cannot enforce resource-ownership invariants at compile time, leaving cost-bearing values aliasable at runtime arXiv:2606.04056; (2) undefined behavior that executes silently in production C/C++ code, generating thousands of warnings even under routine desktop tasks arXiv:2606.12064; (3) numeric format proliferation across ML accelerators that produces silent divergence without a shared bit-exact reference arXiv:2606.09686; (4) SBOM tooling that cannot agree on what a component is, leaving supply-chain blind spots even when all tools are run arXiv:2606.02442; and (5) harness lifecycle debt in LLM-agent systems, where structural defects mask task-level error signals and make conventional monitoring unreliable arXiv:2606.02494. The unifying structural pattern is verification theater: each layer nominally provides a correctness guarantee, but the guarantee is either non-enforceable, scope-limited, or defeated by the layer below it. The falsification path for the thesis is concrete: instrument a single production deployment with all five detection mechanisms simultaneously and measure whether the failure-mode categories are statistically independent, using a chi-squared test of co-occurrence with α = 0.05 as the threshold. If they cluster (reject independence), the structural-deficit framing is supported; if they are independent (fail to reject), the thesis reduces to five unrelated engineering problems. Finite computational resources force a tradeoff between automatic System 1 processes and costly System 2 thinking. Large language models (LLMs) can spend extra computation on hard problems, yet direct answers struggle even with counting, an elementary operation humans and animals perform automatically. We ask why this requires thinking in LLMs. Evidence integration has long been used in psychology and neuroscience to probe decision-making. Our evidence-integration task presents one letter per conversational turn and asks which of two target letters appeared more often. A running count difference solves the task optimally by weighting every letter equally; tokens at each turn could represent and update this difference. Direct responses instead weighted evidence unevenly, with strong recency effects, and assigned less probability to the correct answer as difficulty increased. Thinking improved performance and made integration weights nearly uniform, yet final-query attention remained concentrated on the sequence ends in both modes. Reasoning trajectories showed models revisiting input, recounting letters, and checking intermediate counts that informed the answer, suggesting that thinking constructs the accumulated count that direct responses lack rather than reading out one already formed. Reasoning-token costs grew with the number of letters far more than with coherence. Outcome feedback did not bring this computation into direct responses: under in-context reinforcement learning (ICRL), performance deteriorated over repeated games and recency effects strengthened, yet models grew more confident. Humans and animals amortize such computations into automatic processes, whereas current LLMs still pay for them with thinking on every trial. Which operations learning can make directly available remains central to how future models allocate computation.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used by university students for academic information seeking, explanation, drafting and problem solving. Its usefulness, however, depends not only on ease of use or frequency of interaction but also on users' capacity to evaluate and verify AI-generated information. This study presents an independent secondary-data analysis of a publicly available, anonymised dataset containing responses from 104 university students to 20 five-point Likert-scale items covering perceived ease of use (PEOU), trust in AI, verification behaviour and digital literacy. The analysis examined internal consistency, factorability diagnostics, descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations and multiple linear regression using heteroscedasticity-consistent HC3 standard errors. The four constructs demonstrated acceptable to high internal consistency (Cronbach's α = .782–.898). The KMO measure was .836 and Bartlett's test of sphericity was statistically significant, χ²(190) = 1087.35, p < .001, indicating that the item correlation matrix was suitable for factor-analytic examination. Verification behaviour was positively correlated with AI-related digital literacy (r = .445, p < .001), whereas its bivariate associations with PEOU and trust were not statistically significant. In the multivariable model, AI-related digital literacy showed the largest standardized coefficient (β = .524, p < .001). Trust showed a small negative adjusted association with verification behaviour (β = −.214, p = .048), whereas PEOU and usage frequency were not statistically significant. The model explained 25.3% of the variance in verification behaviour (R² = .253; adjusted R² = .223). The findings suggest that effective academic engagement with GenAI should not be equated with frequent use or perceived ease of use. Instead, evaluative digital-literacy capabilities appear particularly relevant to verification behaviour. Building on these findings, the study proposes the HEAVEN framework (Human-centred Evaluation of AI-generated academic information through Verification, Evidence and Nuanced judgement) as a conceptual framework integrating AI literacy, information verification, evidence appraisal and human judgement in higher education.

documents.abstract: CT Perfusion in Acute Ischemic Stroke Beyond 4.5 Hours: Extending Thrombectomy Window Using Core-Penumbra Mismatch — V1 Synthetic Educational Model Highlighting Collateral Variability and Need for Indian Validation of AI Trained on Foreign Data Authors: Kishore Das (Independent Researcher – Biomedical Engineer, Madhyamgram, Kolkata, India ) Keywords: CT Perfusion, CTP, Core Penumbra Mismatch, Acute Ischemic Stroke, Collateral Circulation, AI Bias, Indian Population, Synthetic Educational Model, Thrombectomy Window, Imaging Biomarker Abstract: Acute ischemic stroke (AIS) due to large vessel occlusion (LVO) causes rapid neuronal death. Intravenous thrombolysis is limited to 4.5 hours, but in India >90% patients present late after 8-12 hours. Objective: 1) To explain CTP physics, 2) To show how CTP extends window from 4.5 hr to 24 hr using Core-Penumbra mismatch, 3) To highlight potential AI bias when AI Trained on Foreign Data auto-perfusion software is applied to Indian population. Methods: This V1 is 100% synthetic educational model only. No patient data, no real CTP scans. All figures are schematic. Protocol: Step 1 NCCT Head to exclude hemorrhage, Step 2 CTA Head and Neck to see LVO ICA/M1, Step 3 CTP. Parameters: 40-50 ml contrast at 5 ml/sec, 60-70 sec scanning at 80 kVp. Four maps: CBF <30% = Core (Dead Brain - Blue Center), CBV low in Core, MTT >6 sec = Penumbra, Tmax >6 sec = Penumbra (At-Risk - Red Yellow Around). Results: Illustrative Hypothetical Synthetic Case (100% Educational - No Real Patient): *Concept: - Core <70 ml = Dead part small - operation possible - Penumbra = At Risk Part - can be saved - Mismatch Ratio = Penumbra / Core >1.8 = Savable part 1.8 times bigger than dead - good - Mismatch Volume >15 ml = At least 15 ml savable tissue must be there *Hypothetical Example (Synthetic Only): A hypothetical patient presents after 8 hours. NCCT Head is normal (plain black-white CT shows nothing common in early stroke). CTP shows Core 25 ml (dead brain part small blue in center cannot be saved) and Penumbra 110 ml (at risk big red-yellow around can be saved if blood returns quickly). Software reported trained on more than 50 perfusion studies from multiple sites (manufacturer reports larger internal datasets; we mention more than 50 with scientific caution). Since training mainly on AI Trained on Foreign Data, bias MAY exist for Indian pattern. Therefore, AI Trained on Foreign Data may need local Indian validation. V2 will test with real de-identified cases with IRB approval. Conclusion: CTP with Core-Penumbra mismatch can extend window from 4.5 hr to 24 hr and opens platform for next-generation medicine design. Sierra Leone is faced with complex energy challenges, including very low rates of access to electricity. Nevertheless, ambitious goals have been set for the country through the Energy Transition and Green Growth Plan. Opportunities for solar energy deployment feature prominently in these goals, although they are clearly imagined in very different ways by the various energy sector actors. Some see large-scale hydropower as the future backbone of the electricity system, with opportunities for deploying solar photovoltaic energy in an auxiliary role. Others emphasise the potential of solar mini-grids. Still others see the greatest potential in household-scale solar systems to meet basic energy needs. In this article, we use the concept of sociotechnical imaginaries to examine these competing narratives. We argue that all of these technologies have their place in the future energy landscape of the country, but the vastly different geographical and economic realities and needs of diverse communities need to be duly considered when shaping the future energy landscape.

Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) have converged on a common assumption: that the communication topology connecting agents is either fixed at design time or left entirely to unconstrained dynamic negotiation. This paper argues, through a heuristic reading of seven recent arXiv preprints spanning cs.MA, cs.DC, and cs.NI, that this binary is a false dichotomy, and that the most effective systems in the corpus share a structural pattern we call deliberate topology selection: the explicit, policy-guided choice of which edges to activate, suppress, or reconfigure at runtime, conditioned on task state, budget, and agent confidence. This is a heuristic reading, not a derivation from a shared formalism; the papers do not share a unified mathematical framework, but they converge on a common engineering diagnosis. The synthesis draws on findings about: training-free communication pruning via Theory-of-Mind confidence signals (arXiv:2605.29612) (a preprint its authors withdrew on 2026-09-22, so its reported results are not relied on here; see the Correction note); task-conditioned structural priors that guide posterior orchestration (arXiv:2605.25746); nucleus-electron hierarchies that separate stable backbones from dynamically activated agents (arXiv:2605.26178); game-theoretic minimax method selection under scenario uncertainty (arXiv:2606.02383); decentralized event-triggered synchronization under censored feedback (arXiv:2605.27076); federated market-based allocation over tree-structured service DAGs (arXiv:2605.27106); and infrastructure-layer topology proposals for V2X safety communication (arXiv:2605.25431). The central falsification path is concrete: if a static, task-agnostic topology trained once on a broad corpus consistently matches or outperforms deliberate topology selection across coordination-heavy benchmarks, the thesis collapses. The abstract reports no such result in any corpus paper; the claim remains a candidate structural pattern worth investigating, not an established law. A recurring structural pattern across recent multi-agent systems (MAS) research is that the mechanism by which agents reach collective decisions, aggregation versus deliberation, produces systematically different reliability and scalability profiles, and that neither mechanism dominates unconditionally. This study examines the role, educational opportunities, and current challenges of integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies into higher education to develop university students' oral communication and foreign language speaking skills. Utilizing natural language processing (NLP), automatic speech recognition (ASR), and large language models (LLMs), the paper establishes a theoretical and practical framework for AI-mediated instruction. Key benefits, such as reducing foreign language speaking anxiety, constructing personalized learning trajectories, offering real-time corrective feedback, and enhancing phonetic accuracy and oral fluency, are analyzed in detail. Furthermore, the paper highlights critical implementation barriers and provides actionable pedagogical guidelines for incorporating AI applications effectively into tertiary curricula.

documents.abstract: This conceptual review examines how digital transformation is reshaping Indian commerce and the world of work that sustains it. Adopting an integrative literature review design, the study synthesises 30 scholarly and institutional sources, comprising foundational theory on technology and organisations, recent evidence on automation and artificial intelligence, and India-focused research and official reports on digitalisation, employment, informality and leadership, through thematic analysis. Four themes emerge: the digitalisation of commercial activity, the recomposition of employment, the centrality of workforce capability and leadership, and the risk of a widening divide between the organised economy and traditional and unorganised sectors. Official estimates place India's digital economy at 11.74% of national income in 2022-23, with a projected share of nearly one-fifth by 2029-30, which underlines the scale of the shift. The synthesis indicates that the employment effects of digitalisation are compositional and not uniformly negative, that returns to digital investment depend on complementary human and organisational capabilities, and that the informal workforce, including handloom producers, construction labour and migrant workers, remains largely outside the digital dividend. The paper integrates these insights into a Digital Commerce–Work–Capability framework and advances five research propositions for empirical testing. It offers practical guidance for business managers, educational institutions and policymakers seeking inclusive digital growth.

The processes in audit firms face operational challenges due to the reliance on manual workflows, particularly in managing audit engagement tasks and tracking auditor training hours. Such inefficiencies lead to an increased administrative burden and potential compliance risks. This work describes our initiatives to address these issues by developing a system that combines a web application to streamline audit engagement monitoring and a mobile application to monitor staff training. Initially designed to replace manual workflows, the system has evolved to incorporate generative artificial intelligence to enhance knowledge retrieval for audit-related queries. The initiatives improve the efficiency of audit engagement and staff training monitoring, enabling audit firms to achieve significant improvements in their workflow.

Ground deformation induced by the touchdown impact of collapsed bodies can adversely affect critical structures and facilities, including adjacent buildings, underground pipelines, and metro tunnels. This study investigates the soil deformation induced by collapsed body impact in two typical strata, namely homogeneous soil and stiff-over-soft strata. We conducted model tests for both strata, and established an experimentally validated numerical model using the LS-DYNA finite element analysis software. We analysed the dynamic response characteristics and energy dissipation patterns of both homogeneous soil and stiff-over-soft strata models under the most unfavorable working conditions of touchdown impact loading. Two methods, namely the force–displacement curve method and the Winkler foundation model, were adopted to predict the energy dissipation during the touchdown impact process. Research findings indicated that the dynamic response characteristics of homogeneous soil models under touchdown impact loading were significantly influenced by distance and depth. The majority (approximately 83.37%) is of the impact energy dissipated through plastic deformation of the soil. In stiff-over-soft strata, due to the confinement effect and ’shell effect’ of the concrete slab, localised failure and crack propagation within the slab dominate system energy dissipation, accounting for approximately 61.63% of the total impact energy. When employing force–displacement curves to predict energy dissipation in models directly subjected to impact, both models demonstrated good agreement with simulation results. However, when using the Winkler foundation model to predict energy dissipation in directly impacted models, the homogeneous soil model showed superior agreement. These findings can provide a valuable reference for the safety assessment and the formulation of protective measures for engineering structures affected by the touchdown impact loading of collapsed bodies.

This study establishes a rigorous mathematical and empirical framework governing the transient state-space deviations from deterministic logical trajectories---conceptually designated as temporary cognitive lapses---observed in Large Language Models (LLMs) under extended context horizons. Grounded in a functionalist paradigm that transitions human-AI interaction into a single, closed-loop symbiotic informatics matrix, we define these lapses as volatile log-probability fluctuations triggered by localized attention hyperpolarization across supersaturated symbolic fields. Unlike permanent structural hallucinations, the real-time injection of human-guided subsegmentation commands operates as an exogenous homeostatic forcing operator---termed a cognitive pulse. This external impulse perturbs the key-value (KV) cache history matrix via entry-wise Hadamard modulation, forcing an exact singular value condensation that flattens distorted log-probability landscapes. Consequently, the diffuse probability mass is compressed, executing an instantaneous non-continuous vertical trajectory jump that re-orients the hidden representation vectors back onto canonical factual state attractors. We provide quantitative theoretical predictions tracking these transitions across all operational co-evolutionary interaction phases, establishing a rigorous mathematical baseline for co-evolutionary intelligence survival. Contemporary fiscal architectures rely overwhelmingly on human labor income and payroll withholdings to finance social insurance and public infrastructure. The rapid diffusion of autonomous software agents, generative foundation models, and embodied robotic systems decouples output growth from human work hours, eroding traditional tax bases while exacerbating capital-income concentration. Prevailing policy proposals, ranging from uniform robot levies to unconditional cash transfers, fail to resolve three foundational challenges: attributing economic value across mixed human-machine workflows, establishing legal fiscal liability without creating fictional machine personhood, and building an equitable distribution mechanism that converts technological surplus into durable public wealth. This paper presents CivicDividendOS, an end-to-end computational fiscal framework for mixed human-AIrobot economies. The architecture introduces an Autonomous Economic Activity Passport (AEAP) that anchors machine activity to accountable corporate beneficiaries, paired with a Factor-Origin Ledger (FOL) that calculates causal marginal contributions across labor, AI services, robotics, data, and conventional capital. Drawing on an endogenous Substitution-Augmentation Classifier, the system levies a dynamic Social Automation Contribution (SAC) on automated value added, offering explicit offset credits for worker upskilling, augmentation, and task innovation. Accrued revenues are recycled through a Human Earned-Income Shield (HEIS) to reduce payroll wedges and a Public Automation Wealth Fund (PAWF) whose structural yields endow citizen dividends, transition insurance, and human capabilities. We formalize the mathematical architecture, illustrate its operation in an urban logistics setting, and outline an evaluation protocol via a macroeconomic policy digital twin.

documents.abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have emerged as transformative technologies that enable direct communication between the brain and external devices. Among various BCI paradigms, EEG-based motor imagery (MI) has gained prominence due to its simplicity, non-invasiveness, and potential to restore motor function and facilitate rehabilitation for patients with motor impairments. This paper presents a comprehensive review of the most practical processing algorithms developed over the past decade for decoding brain sensorimotor cortex signals. Specifically, this paper discusses the integration of artificial intelligence (AI)-based algorithms, particularly machine learning and deep learning techniques, and their contributions to improving the performance and efficiency of MI-BCI systems in detail. Furthermore, the paper reviews state-of-the-art hardware platforms and emerging converging technologies, including system-on-chip (SoC) architectures, application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), wearable devices, the Internet of Things (IoT), and augmented/virtual reality (AR/VR), and discusses their integration with advanced signal processing algorithms to enable next-generation MI-BCI systems. By highlighting current achievements of EEG-based MI-BCI technology and predicting future research directions that could further enhance real-time capabilities, this paper aims to provide valuable insights for researchers and practitioners, fostering innovation in high-performance EEG-based MI-BCI systems.

Este ensayo examina la discrepancia entre la alfabetización técnica en inteligencia artificial y la preservación del juicio deliberativo, introduciendo el concepto de analfabetismo de agencia. Frente a marcos normativos como el Artículo 4 del Reglamento de Inteligencia Artificial de la Unión Europea, se analiza la falacia del «human-in-the-loop» como un mecanismo de legitimación burocrática y exculpación jurídica mediante el análisis empírico del sistema MCAS del Boeing 737 MAX. Finalmente, se proponen dos salvaguardas operativas indispensables para el autogobierno sociotécnico: la reserva operacional y el oficio de responder. ---This essay examines the gap between technical artificial intelligence literacy and the preservation of deliberative judgment, introducing the concept of agency illiteracy. In light of regulatory frameworks such as Article 4 of the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, it analyzes the fallacy of the "human-in-the-loop" as an instrument of bureaucratic legitimation and legal exculpation through the empirical case of the Boeing 737 MAX MCAS system. Finally, it proposes two indispensable operational safeguards for sociotechnical self-governance: operational reserve and the craft of answering (moral accountability).

documents.abstract: Este trabajo formaliza el ensayo de suficiencia como un protocolo de auditoría sociotécnica concebido para verificar la autonomía operativa y el discernimiento deliberativo en entornos de alta mediación computacional. Frente a métricas convencionales que premian la velocidad del binomio humano–máquina bajo asistencia ininterrumpida, se fundamenta el principio de «evaluación por sustracción» con salvaguardas explícitas de contención de riesgo. Se reelabora la noción de competencia parasitaria no como una deficiencia individual o culposa del operador, sino como una propiedad emergente de configuraciones institucionales que incentivan la delegación epistémica y restringen el acceso a los fundamentos del sistema. A partir de los marcos de la ingeniería de resiliencia (Hollnagel, Woods) y de la práctica de la ingeniería del caos ya consolidada en sistemas distribuidos, el ensayo desarrolla un protocolo estructurado en cuatro vectores normativos —continuidad esencial, degradación comprensible, suficiencia material y agencia verificable—, contextualiza el caso histórico del MCAS en la aviación civil como referencia documental sobre asimetría informativa y degradación inadvertida, y propone criterios de gobernanza aplicables a proyectos e infraestructuras críticas. ---This paper formalizes the "sufficiency test" as a sociotechnical auditing protocol designed to verify operational autonomy and deliberative judgment in highly mediated computational environments. In contrast to conventional performance metrics that reward human–machine throughput under continuous algorithmic assistance, it operationalizes the principle of "evaluation by subtraction" within explicit containment boundaries. The concept of parasitic competence is redefined not as an individual moral or technical failing, but as an emergent property of sociotechnical configurations that incentivize epistemic offloading while restricting structural access and deliberative authority. Grounded in resilience engineering frameworks (Hollnagel, Woods) and in the already-established practice of chaos engineering in distributed systems, the essay formulates a structured testing protocol across four normative vectors—essential continuity, understandable degradation, material sufficiency, and verifiable agency—, examines the MCAS civil aviation case as an illustrative documentary reference on information asymmetry and unannounced degradation, and outlines governance mechanisms for critical infrastructure and project management.

documents.abstract: La investigación titulada “El uso de ChatGPT y su impacto sobre las habilidades críticas del pensamiento en estudiantes universitarios de la región Puno, 2024” tuvo como propósito determinar si el uso de la inteligencia artificial, específicamente ChatGPT, se relaciona con el pensamiento crítico de los estudiantes universitarios de la región Puno. El estudio surge ante la incorporación acelerada de la inteligencia artificial en el ámbito educativo y la preocupación de que, si bien ChatGPT puede facilitar el acceso a información, apoyar la realización de tareas y proporcionar respuestas rápidas, su utilización excesiva podría disminuir la necesidad de que los estudiantes analicen, cuestionen, evalúen y resuelvan problemas de manera autónoma. En este sentido, los autores identificaron como problemática la limitada evidencia existente sobre la relación entre ChatGPT y las habilidades de pensamiento crítico en estudiantes universitarios de la región Puno, considerando que investigaciones previas habían abordado principalmente los efectos de la inteligencia artificial sobre procesos cognitivos y metacognitivos de manera general. El estudio se desarrolló bajo un enfoque cuantitativo, correspondiendo a una investigación empírica con estrategia asociativa y diseño correlacional de corte transversal, debido a que buscó examinar estadísticamente la relación entre las variables sin manipularlas y mediante la recolección de información en un momento determinado. La población estuvo conformada por estudiantes universitarios del departamento de Puno, provenientes de diferentes áreas académicas, y se planteó inicialmente una muestra de 500 estudiantes con edades principalmente comprendidas entre los 18 y 30 años; finalmente, participaron 512 estudiantes universitarios, de los cuales el 53.1 % fueron mujeres y el 46.8 % hombres. Asimismo, el 97.4 % manifestó conocer ChatGPT y el 97.2 % señaló haber utilizado esta herramienta. El muestreo empleado fue no probabilístico por conveniencia, por lo que los resultados deben interpretarse considerando las características específicas de los participantes y no como evidencia necesariamente generalizable a toda la población universitaria de Puno. Para evaluar la variable relacionada con ChatGPT se utilizó el Cuestionario de ChatGPT de Oros (2024), compuesto por 20 ítems organizados en las dimensiones de Fluidez, Flexibilidad y Originalidad, con respuestas en una escala Likert de cinco niveles; el instrumento presentó una consistencia interna global de α = .830 y ω = .829. Para evaluar el pensamiento crítico se empleó un cuestionario de 34 ítems compuesto por seis dimensiones: Interpretación, Análisis, Inferencia, Evaluación, Explicación y Autorregulación, cuya consistencia interna global alcanzó α = .902 y ω = .902. El procesamiento estadístico se realizó mediante JASP, utilizando estadísticos descriptivos, análisis de asimetría y curtosis, prueba de normalidad de Kolmogórov-Smirnov y el coeficiente Rho de Spearman para analizar la relación entre las variables. Los resultados mostraron que la percepción de ChatGPT fue predominantemente favorable, debido a que el 76.5 % de los participantes presentó una percepción buena y el 12.8 % una percepción muy buena; sin embargo, esta percepción positiva no implicó una relación significativa con el pensamiento crítico. El resultado principal evidenció una correlación prácticamente nula entre ChatGPT y el pensamiento crítico global (Rho = −.010; p = .830), por lo que no se encontró evidencia estadísticamente significativa de una asociación entre ambas variables. Del mismo modo, al analizar las dimensiones específicas del pensamiento crítico, tampoco se encontraron relaciones estadísticamente significativas con ChatGPT: Interpretación (Rho = −.047; p = .291), Análisis (Rho = −.055; p = .218), Inferencia (Rho = .035; p = .430), Evaluación (Rho = −.016; p = .711), Explicación (Rho = .041; p = .357) y Autorregulación (Rho = −.030; p = .498). Aunque se identificó una asociación estadísticamente significativa entre la dimensión de Fluidez de ChatGPT y la dimensión de Inferencia del pensamiento crítico (Rho = .090; p = .042), su magnitud fue muy baja y constituye un resultado específico entre dimensiones, por lo que no modifica el resultado general de ausencia de relación significativa entre las variables principales. En la discusión, los autores plantean que ChatGPT puede constituir una herramienta útil para facilitar el acceso a información, apoyar actividades académicas, generar ideas y permitir la exploración de diferentes perspectivas; no obstante, también señalan que un uso excesivamente dependiente podría representar un riesgo para procesos como el análisis, la evaluación y la autorregulación del aprendizaje. Sin embargo, es importante precisar que tales riesgos corresponden principalmente a planteamientos teóricos y antecedentes discutidos en el artículo, ya que los datos obtenidos en esta investigación no demostraron una relación estadísticamente significativa entre el uso de ChatGPT y un aumento o disminución del pensamiento crítico. Entre las principales limitaciones se reconoce que el diseño correlacional y transversal no permite establecer relaciones causales; además, el muestreo por conveniencia limita la generalización de los resultados, la investigación se concentró exclusivamente en estudiantes de la región Puno y se estudió únicamente ChatGPT, sin incorporar otras herramientas de inteligencia artificial que también podrían estar relacionadas con los procesos cognitivos de los estudiantes. En conclusión, la investigación encontró que, dentro de la muestra de 512 estudiantes universitarios analizada, el uso de ChatGPT no presentó una relación estadísticamente significativa con el pensamiento crítico global ni con sus dimensiones de interpretación, análisis, inferencia, evaluación, explicación y autorregulación, por lo que los resultados no permiten afirmar que ChatGPT mejore o deteriore el pensamiento crítico; únicamente indican que, bajo las condiciones, instrumentos, población y diseño empleados, no se encontró una asociación estadísticamente significativa entre ambas variables.

El estudio surge ante la incorporación acelerada de la inteligencia artificial en el ámbito educativo y la preocupación de que, si bien ChatGPT puede facilitar el acceso a información, apoyar la realización de tareas y proporcionar respuestas rápidas, su utilización excesiva podría disminuir la necesidad de que los estudiantes analicen, cuestionen, evalúen y resuelvan problemas de manera autónoma. En este sentido, los autores identificaron como problemática la limitada evidencia existente sobre la relación entre ChatGPT y las habilidades de pensamiento crítico en estudiantes universitarios de la región Puno, considerando que investigaciones previas habían abordado principalmente los efectos de la inteligencia artificial sobre procesos cognitivos y metacognitivos de manera general. El estudio se desarrolló bajo un enfoque cuantitativo, correspondiendo a una investigación empírica con estrategia asociativa y diseño correlacional de corte transversal, debido a que buscó examinar estadísticamente la relación entre las variables sin manipularlas y mediante la recolección de información en un momento determinado. La población estuvo conformada por estudiantes universitarios del departamento de Puno, provenientes de diferentes áreas académicas, y se planteó inicialmente una muestra de 500 estudiantes con edades principalmente comprendidas entre los 18 y 30 años; finalmente, participaron 512 estudiantes universitarios, de los cuales el 53.1 % fueron mujeres y el 46.8 % hombres. Asimismo, el 97.4 % manifestó conocer ChatGPT y el 97.2 % señaló haber utilizado esta herramienta. El muestreo empleado fue no probabilístico por conveniencia, por lo que los resultados deben interpretarse considerando las características específicas de los participantes y no como evidencia necesariamente generalizable a toda la población universitaria de Puno. Para evaluar la variable relacionada con ChatGPT se utilizó el Cuestionario de ChatGPT de Oros (2024), compuesto por 20 ítems organizados en las dimensiones de Fluidez, Flexibilidad y Originalidad, con respuestas en una escala Likert de cinco niveles; el instrumento presentó una consistencia interna global de α = .830 y ω = .829. Para evaluar el pensamiento crítico se empleó un cuestionario de 34 ítems compuesto por seis dimensiones: Interpretación, Análisis, Inferencia, Evaluación, Explicación y Autorregulación, cuya consistencia interna global alcanzó α = .902 y ω = .902. El procesamiento estadístico se realizó mediante JASP, utilizando estadísticos descriptivos, análisis de asimetría y curtosis, prueba de normalidad de Kolmogórov-Smirnov y el coeficiente Rho de Spearman para analizar la relación entre las variables. Los resultados mostraron que la percepción de ChatGPT fue predominantemente favorable, debido a que el 76.5 % de los participantes presentó una percepción buena y el 12.8 % una percepción muy buena; sin embargo, esta percepción positiva no implicó una relación significativa con el pensamiento crítico. El resultado principal evidenció una correlación prácticamente nula entre ChatGPT y el pensamiento crítico global (Rho = −.010; p = .830), por lo que no se encontró evidencia estadísticamente significativa de una asociación entre ambas variables. Del mismo modo, al analizar las dimensiones específicas del pensamiento crítico, tampoco se encontraron relaciones estadísticamente significativas con ChatGPT: Interpretación (Rho = −.047; p = .291), Análisis (Rho = −.055; p = .218), Inferencia (Rho = .035; p = .430), Evaluación (Rho = −.016; p = .711), Explicación (Rho = .041; p = .357) y Autorregulación (Rho = −.030; p = .498). Aunque se identificó una asociación estadísticamente significativa entre la dimensión de Fluidez de ChatGPT y la dimensión de Inferencia del pensamiento crítico (Rho = .090; p = .042), su magnitud fue muy baja y constituye un resultado específico entre dimensiones, por lo que no modifica el resultado general de ausencia de relación significativa entre las variables principales. En la discusión, los autores plantean que ChatGPT puede constituir una herramienta útil para facilitar el acceso a información, apoyar actividades académicas, generar ideas y permitir la exploración de diferentes perspectivas; no obstante, también señalan que un uso excesivamente dependiente podría representar un riesgo para procesos como el análisis, la evaluación y la autorregulación del aprendizaje. Sin embargo, es importante precisar que tales riesgos corresponden principalmente a planteamientos teóricos y antecedentes discutidos en el artículo, ya que los datos obtenidos en esta investigación no demostraron una relación estadísticamente significativa entre el uso de ChatGPT y un aumento o disminución del pensamiento crítico. Entre las principales limitaciones se reconoce que el diseño correlacional y transversal no permite establecer relaciones causales; además, el muestreo por conveniencia limita la generalización de los resultados, la investigación se concentró exclusivamente en estudiantes de la región Puno y se estudió únicamente ChatGPT, sin incorporar otras herramientas de inteligencia artificial que también podrían estar relacionadas con los procesos cognitivos de los estudiantes. En conclusión, la investigación encontró que, dentro de la muestra de 512 estudiantes universitarios analizada, el uso de ChatGPT no presentó una relación estadísticamente significativa con el pensamiento crítico global ni con sus dimensiones de interpretación, análisis, inferencia, evaluación, explicación y autorregulación, por lo que los resultados no permiten afirmar que ChatGPT mejore o deteriore el pensamiento crítico; únicamente indican que, bajo las condiciones, instrumentos, población y diseño empleados, no se encontró una asociación estadísticamente significativa entre ambas variables.

documents.abstract: The neural scaling law relating longer training to better performance through a power law is central to today's large language models (LLMs), yet its origin remains debated. One recent proposal is that power laws can emerge from the strong non-linearity of a single softmax head learning peaked distributions. What happens with multiple softmax functions, as in LLMs, is unclear. Here, we show through toy models that any softmax learning peaked distributions, regardless of its position in the model, can develop logit magnitudes that grow in a power law with exponent $1/3$, becoming a training bottleneck whose loss contribution decays as a power law with the same exponent $1/3$. The overall loss therefore obeys $1/3$ scaling whenever at least one softmax learns peaked distributions. We confirm that many softmax functions in LLMs learn peaked distributions and that LLM loss scaling matches this $1/3$ prediction. Moreover, logit growth dynamics reveal that attention heads, rather than the language modeling head, are the bottleneck likely driving the $1/3$ loss scaling in LLMs. Attention trying to concentrate on specific information, which is the heart of Transformers, may therefore also be the heart of the neural scaling law of training.

Hybrid attention models have emerged as a crucial architecture for Large Language Models (LLMs) (e.g., the Qwen3.5 and Kimi series). Their memory and computational efficiency make them highly attractive for on-device inference, forming a promising synergy with edge Neural Processing Units (NPUs). However, naive execution of these hybrid models on edge NPUs fails to deliver these benefits, often bottlenecking the prefill stage due to severe memory-system inefficiencies and architectural mismatches within the linear attention (LA) layers. We present HA-NPU, the first system to enable efficient hybrid attention LLM inference on edge NPUs without modifying the underlying algorithms. HA-NPU enhances execution efficiency by reorganizing the dataflow of the LA components across three levels: (1) At the core level, it partitions workloads by the head dimension and fuses dependent operators, eliminating cross-core global memory accesses; (2) At the operator level, it reorders execution to consume intermediate tensors immediately, drastically minimizing local-buffer pressure; (3) At the tensor level, it employs dataflow-aware layout planning to minimize transformation overhead between matrix and vector processing units. Compared to competitive baselines, HA-NPU achieves up to 35.95$\times$ LA kernel speedup and 36.14$\times$ energy reduction, delivering up to 2.03$\times$ faster end-to-end request latency. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/yinyuanzhang/HA-NPU

Unsafe behaviours among hydropower station personnel contribute to accidents and are closely associated with ergonomic risks. To address inefficient manual monitoring and limited consideration of behavioural risks in safety management, this study proposes an improved YOLOv11n-based method for unsafe behaviour detection and develops an ergonomic risk assessment framework using detection results. The method incorporates PConv, an attention mechanism, and Focal Loss into YOLOv11n and integrates YOLOv11n-Pose and DCNN-SE modules to identify unsafe behaviours involving personal protection and actions. Experimental results demonstrate improvements over the comparison model in precision, recall, mean average precision, and inference speed, with robustness to complex backgrounds, small targets, and partial occlusion.

This article examines what effects the use of learning machines may have on human imagination and learning. The narrative of Perseus and Medusa, revisited by Ítalo Calvino, is the image that guides the inquiry: when confronting the Gorgon, the shield protects the gaze and, at the same time, offers an indirect form of approach. From this image, we ask whether generative artificial intelligence tends to petrify thought — by offering answers that precede the effort of creation — or whether it can function as a mediation that broadens perspectives. This is a qualitative, bibliographical and exploratory study, conducted as a theoretical essay of philosophical-educational interpretation. The discussion articulates lightness and visibility in Calvino, Nietzsche's critique of education subordinated to haste and utility, the notion of symbolic forms in Cassirer, and Maxine Greene's educational imagination. The analysis shows that technology does not determine, by itself, either the impoverishment or the expansion of imagination. The risk arises when the automated response takes the place of the student's questioning, hesitation and elaboration. We conclude that artificial intelligence can serve learning when it remains as a shield: a questioned, limited mediation subordinated to human authorship.

Multi-agent LLM systems are increasingly deployed in consequential settings, network diagnostics, clinical reasoning, financial oracles, robotic control, yet their failure modes remain poorly characterised at the system level. This paper advances a candidate structural reading: that degradation in multi-agent LLM systems is not primarily a function of individual model quality but emerges from the interaction of four compounding mechanisms operating across the coordination stack. We identify these as (1) entropy accumulation from intrinsic agent properties that grow monotonically with interaction rounds, (2) communication inefficiency arising from redundant token generation and poorly structured information exchange, (3) deliberation pathology in which consensus mechanisms propagate rather than correct errors, and (4) censored feedback that prevents agents from distinguishing coordination failure from stochastic task failure. Drawing on findings from cs.MA and cs.DC preprints, we argue, as a heuristic reading, not a formal derivation, that these four mechanisms occupy distinct layers of the coordination stack but interact in ways that make system-level degradation substantially harder to diagnose than any single-layer failure. The thesis generates concrete falsification paths: the entropy growth rate α should be measurable and architecture-dependent; communication efficiency gains should be separable from accuracy gains in ablation; deliberation accuracy should correlate negatively with inter-model error correlation; and censored-feedback regret should decompose into structural-search and statistical-monitoring terms with distinct scaling behaviours. We argue that treating these mechanisms as jointly constitutive of a degradation topology, rather than as independent bugs, motivates a candidate class of system-level monitoring primitives. The abstract reports empirical findings from the cited preprints; whether the interaction effects generalise beyond the specific architectures and benchmarks studied is open. Foundation models have recently shown strong potential for learning generalizable EEG representations, yet their effectiveness for event-related potential (ERP) analysis remains unclear. In this work, we investigate two fundamental questions: 1) can foundation-model learning benefit ERP analysis, and what limits the transfer of existing EEG foundation models to ERP tasks? 2) can the complementary advantages of single-trial and averaged-trial ERP be integrated into a unified training pipeline? To study these questions, we curate a large-scale ERP corpus comprising 1,517,157 single-trial ERPs from 3,696 subjects across 38 datasets and 18 paradigms. Leveraging this corpus, we introduce ERP-FM, to the best of our knowledge, the first foundation model specifically developed for ERP representation learning. ERP-FM uses single-channel tokenization, temporal and spatial positional embeddings, and mixed masked autoencoding for large-scale single-trial pretraining. We compare our model against 17 existing methods on 12 downstream datasets covering ERP event/condition classification and neurological disease classification. Our model achieves the best overall average rank across all evaluated methods. Furthermore, our analyses reveal that both ERP and non-ERP EEG pretraining can provide transferable representations for ERP tasks, while fine-grained temporal tokenization is critical for effectively modeling transient ERP dynamics. We further find that single-trial and averaged-trial ERP play complementary rather than competing roles. Combining single-trial pretraining with averaged-trial downstream adaptation substantially improves neurological disease analysis. Overall, these findings establish an effective foundation-model training pipeline for ERP analysis and represent significant progress toward generalizable ERP representation learning. Psychoeducational reports translate assessment data into decisions about eligibility, services, and instruction, yet research documents persistent problems with their clarity, data-linkage, and usefulness to families and educators (Hale & Brown-Chidsey, 2023; Hite, 2026). Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has entered report writing, and early studies describe its adoption and effects on report quality (Farmer, Lockwood, Floyd, & Sisco, 2025; Lockwood, Farmer et al., 2025). School psychology lacks a structured way to determine when AI assistance is useful, equitable, and defensible and when it introduces risk. This conceptual article proposes a framework organized around three domains: utility, equity, and legal and ethical defensibility. Utility concerns whether reports help intended users understand and act on findings. Equity concerns whether reports improve access while avoiding bias, deficit framing, and unsupported cultural assumptions. Legal and ethical defensibility concerns whether reports preserve practitioner judgment, protect student information, and remain consistent with special education law and professional ethics. The framework considers both where AI is used in a report and the specific task it performs. It supports distinguishing lower-risk from higher-risk uses and informs a proposed risk-stratification system and decision pathway. Implications for practice, training, governance, and research across school psychology are discussed.

documents.abstract: Central Research Question: To what extent do frontier commercial and open-weight large language models (LLMs) accurately assign Emergency Severity Index (ESI) triage tiers to acute psychiatric presentations, and how reliably do their safety guardrails trigger without generating clinically hazardous medical hallucinations? Primary Objectives: 1. Benchmark the emergency triage concordance (ESI Levels 1–5) of frontier LLMs against an expert consensus gold standard established by board-certified emergency psychiatrists across 48 stratified synthetic vignettes. 2. Quantify safety guardrail activation rates (crisis hotline redirection, self-harm protocol engagement, and refusal appropriateness) across active self-harm, command hallucinations, and acute agitation presentations. 3. Measure the frequency, severity, and clinical risk level of model hallucinations, categorizing outputs into factual fabrication, phantom pharmacological recommendations, and diagnostic contraindications. Methodological Framework: This in silico audit tests deterministic (temperature = 0.0) prompt chains across frontier model APIs. The 48-vignette benchmark encompasses four clinical domains: (a) Acute Suicidality and Self-Harm, (b) Psychosis and Catatonia, (c) Neuropsychiatric Toxicity and Delirium, and (d) Severe Agitation and Violence Risk. The 48 synthetic vignettes and clinical evaluation rubrics are archived and frozen within this registration workspace prior to automated API evaluation.

Large language models (LLMs) are being integrated into clinical environments where deference to authority can cause harm. Following an unsafe instruction represents a distinct safety failure. Whether a brief safety reminder changes this behavior is an important clinical safety question. We evaluated 20 open-weight LLMs across 10,096,800 outputs from 601 instances: 501 synthetic variants derived from 50 templates and 100 MIMIC-IV-derived cases. Each instance was tested across 21 framing cells, four mitigation cells, and ten repetitions. The primary outcome was selection of an overtly or partially unsafe option (A or B). We also measured mapped-category consistency across matched ten-run cells. Here we show that 1.18 million of 10.1 million outputs (11.7%) select a potentially harmful option. Selections decrease from 16.6% without mitigation to 10.1% with mitigation (absolute reduction, 6.5 percentage points; p < 0.001), with reductions in synthetic vignettes (10.6% to 7.2%) and MIMIC-IV-derived cases (46.6% to 24.5%). Potentially harmful option selection decreases in 19 of 20 models. Across 1,009,680 matched ten-run cells, 80.4% return the same response category in all ten repetitions; model-level consistency ranges from 4.4% to 100.0%. Among inconsistent cells, 38.2% vary between potentially harmful and safe categories. A safety reminder reduces, but does not eliminate, potentially harmful option selection across both datasets and 19 of 20 models. Category consistency varies across models. This proof-of-concept study provides an evaluation framework but does not estimate clinical risk in deployed systems. Artificial intelligence models used in the hospital may receive instructions that conflict with patient safety. We tested 20 large language models using synthetic cases and records from real clinical recommendations. Each model chose among two potentially harmful and two safe actions, with or without a short reminder to verify or escalate unsafe requests. Across more than 10 million responses, potentially harmful choices fell from 16.6% without the reminder to 10.1% with it. The reduction occurred in 19 of 20 models. In 80.4% of tests that repeated the same case under the same conditions, a model selected the same type of action in all ten repetitions, with almost no difference with or without the reminder. These experiments show how safety reminders in the instructions given to models and consistency of their choices can be evaluated together. They do not show how often harm would occur in clinical practice.

documents.abstract: DNA methylation (DNAM) profiling has emerged as a powerful diagnostic tool for classifying brain and solid tumors. However, existing computational models typically analyze methylation and copy number variation (CNV) data separately, failing to capture the complementary information their integration could provide. Moreover, current classification models lack mechanisms for within-class risk assessment analogous to traditional tumor grading, and no established explainability method can attribute classification decisions to specific genomic loci. In this paper, we present MOXAI (Multi-Omics Based Explainable AI), a deep learning framework that integrates DNA methylation and copy number data from methylation arrays to classify molecular subtypes of adult-type diffuse gliomas, alongside single-modality variants for comparison. Using a cohort from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), we trained ResNet50, DINOv2, and Graph Attention Network (GAT) models on methylation data alone, copy number data alone, and combined multimodal data. We further developed explainable AI (XAI) methods based on class activation maps (CAMs) and gradient-weighted CAM (Grad-CAM) to identify the specific CpG sites, genes, and chromosomal regions most relevant to each classification decision. The multimodal model achieved up to 92.98% cross-validation accuracy, outperforming models trained on CNV data alone. DINOv2 showed the strongest generalization, reaching 94.25% accuracy (confidence >0.9) on independent validation sets. XAI results aligned with established molecular features of adult-type diffuse glioma subtypes, confirming the biological interpretability of the framework.

Purpose Grounded in cognitive load theory and dual process theory, this study aims to investigate how cognitive complexity and health information literacy (HIL) influence users’ cognitive load, perceived learning and cognitive system utilization when acquiring health-related knowledge through artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) and user-generated content (UGC). It aims to reveal cognitive mechanisms underlying these processes and inform improvements in the health information environment. Design/methodology/approach A 2 (learning tools: AIGC vs UGC) × 2 (cognitive complexity: high vs low) × 2 (HIL: high vs low) experimental design was adopted. Data were collected through a questionnaire and evaluated using analysis of variance. Findings Users experienced significant differences in intrinsic and extraneous cognitive load and across all dimensions of perceived learning when using AIGC compared with UGC; Task complexity caused significant differences across all types of cognitive load; HIL levels significantly affected intrinsic and germane cognitive load. Regarding cognitive system utilization, no significant differences emerged between AIGC and UGC. However, higher task complexity increased System 2 engagement universally, and users with higher HIL relied more on System 2 (analytical processing). Originality/value This study develops an integrated framework for examining how learning tools, cognitive complexity and HIL jointly shape learning effectiveness in digital environments. It advances understanding of cognitive processing in digital learning contexts and provides actionable insights for designing cognitively adaptive AIGC and UGC systems.

Exploring Teleoperator Perception through Kinesthetic Feedback Background: Kinesthetic feedback is essential for effective teleoperation, enabling users to perceive and manipulate remote or virtual environments with precision. Haptic codecs exploit human perception thresholds to compress kinesthetic signals, reducing transmission load, but the resulting degradation —together with network-induced delay — may affect both perception and task performance. This work investigates how deadband-based compression and temporal delay jointly influence human performance in teleoperated tasks. Methods: Participants performed two teleoperated tasks under varying levels of deadband compression and network delay. In a letter tracing task, participants traced a reference shape while position and force errors were recorded. In a stiffness discrimination task, participants compared the stiffness of a test spring against soft and stiff reference springs and rated the test stimulus on a four-point scale. Preliminary Results: In the letter tracing task, tracing accuracy declined systematically and monotonically with both increasing compression and increasing delay, with position and force errors rising substantially across the tested parameter range and the largest degradation observed under combined high compression and delay. Degradation was gradual rather than abrupt, with no indication of a threshold beyond which performance broke down. In the stiffness discrimination task, perceived stiffness decreased with increasing delay, consistent with earlier reports. Compression level had no measurable effect on stiffness judgments. Preliminary Conclusion: Kinesthetic codecs enable effective teleoperation under time delay, but performance degrades with increasing compression and delay, and the two tasks showed distinct sensitivity profiles: error-based metrics in a fine motor tracing task were sensitive to both compression and delay, whereas comparative stiffness judgments were sensitive only to delay. These findings suggest that the impact of haptic signal compression and network delay on teleoperator performance is task-dependent, and that codec and network requirements should be tailored to the task at hand.

This study explored the attitudes and experiences of older adults who had used Wearable Physical Activity Monitoring Technology (WPAMT) for at least 30 days, identifying factors influencing continued use and discontinuation. Employing grounded theory, face-to-face interviews with 31 older adults in Hong Kong revealed that most participants held positive attitudes towards WPAMT and a willingness to continue using it. Five determinants largely affected positive attitudes: perceived usefulness, versatility, importance, convenience and effectiveness. Negative attitudes were associated with perceptions of the technology being challenging, unnecessary and unaffordable. Continued use of WPAMT was motivated by utilitarian outcomes, health awareness, trust and the presence of facilitators. Conversely, discontinuation of WPAMT use was associated with technophobia, technological barriers, risk perception and perceived cost.

The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) has impacted various fields, including education. In the context of foreign language (FL) learning, AI tools are increasingly being adopted by both instructors and students to facilitate the teaching and learning processes. This qualitative study explores the utilization of AI tools by English as a Foreign Language (EFL) postgraduate students at the Libyan Academy to enhance their academic writing skills. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with 10 MA and PhD students in Applied Linguistics and analyzed using thematic analysis. The analysis revealed several key themes: the types of AI tools engaged, perceived benefits, encountered challenges, ethical considerations, and skill development. Findings indicate that students employ a diverse range of AI tools, with levels of dependency varying from limited consultation for specific tasks to heavy reliance for completing various writing assignments. While participants acknowledged significant benefits, particularly in enhancing their writing proficiency, they also reported drawbacks, such as limited access to premium versions of AI applications. The study concludes with recommendations for policymakers, instructors, and students, emphasizing the need for clear institutional guidelines on AI use, initiatives to raise student awareness of its ethical application, and efforts to mitigate challenges that could otherwise passively hinder the development of academic writing skills.

documents.abstract: Learning from experience in LLM agents has become a key paradigm for developing self-evolving agents that continuously learn and expand their capabilities. Within this paradigm, synthesizing the agent skill has emerged as a promising solution for transforming accumulated experience into reusable procedural knowledge, serving as an important layer for the harness system that supplies agents at runtime. Despite its potential, existing approaches largely abstract past experience into fixed procedural knowledge before downstream demands are known, which risks discarding knowledge that later becomes critical while retaining instance-specific details irrelevant to future tasks. In this paper, we reframe agent skill synthesis as a dynamic navigation problem over past experience, where agents actively explore accumulated trajectories on demand for the current task with targeted and fine-grained access to experience knowledge. To this end, we propose ExpVoyager, a novel framework in which a skill curator navigates raw experience across different views and resolutions, continually identifying reusable procedural knowledge from what it observes while tracking remaining knowledge needs that guide where to navigate next. Extensive experiments demonstrate both the effectiveness and versatility of ExpVoyager, showing consistent improvements in downstream task performance, continual gains as the experience space scales, and practical compatibility with existing skills under efficient experience access.

documents.abstract: Virtual reality (VR) technology is a valuable tool to address the evolving needs of young-old adults. This study investigated the factors influencing the adoption of VR technology among young-old adults, extending the technology acceptance model by incorporating trust and perceived risk. Data were collected from 343 respondents aged 60 and above through a structured questionnaire, with structural equation modelling used for data analysis. The findings revealed that trust plays a central role in shaping young-old adults' attitudes towards VR technology and their behavioural intentions to adopt it. Additionally, perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness positively contribute to the formation of trust. Conversely, perceived safety risk and performance risk negatively affect trust.

The development of generative AI (GAI) capabilities has led corporate entities to rethink their strategic initiatives towards sustainable workforce management. This dynamism has been broadly identified as a concern for managerial teams. Despite strong consensus on the roles of organizational human resources and corporate governance in managing the deployment of GAI mechanisms, specific factors contributing to each orientation remain unidentified. The current study addresses this gap by conducting a comprehensive review of factors that may affect sustainability orientation and employee well-being in the context of GAI implementation. The study utilized total interpretive structural modeling (TISM) and cross-impact matrix multiplication applied to the classification (MICMAC) method to develop the hierarchical relationship model. The study identified 16 factors: nine attributed to human resource management (HRM) and seven to the corporate social responsibility (CSR) domain. The study develops an expert-informed structural representation of the interrelationships between the two categories of designated factors. The outcomes identify two foundational factors as independent drivers and one dependent factor related to the social assessment of technology from a CSR perspective. The findings provide a structured interpretation of the interdependence between HRM and CSR factors and their implications for sustainable workforce management and employee health in SMEs. The study offers novel managerial implications on the relative orientations of driving and dependency factors for managing a sustainable workforce while supporting new technology development in the SME context.

Objective This study aimed to evaluate characteristics, first aid and PPE use among patients with occupational corneal foreign body (CFB) injuries.Methods A cross-sectional study included 92 male patients treated at Harran University. Data on demographics, job type, injury cause, PPE use, first aid and occupational safety service exposure were analysed.Results The mean age was 36.04 ± 12.24 years, average work experience 11.86 ± 10.98 years. Welding/metalwork was the most common job (38.0%), and 87.0% of injuries were caused by metallic objects. Treatment delay occurred in 75.0% of patients, incorrect first aid was reported in 9.8%, and 53.3% did not consistently use PPE. Younger patients performed significantly better first aid (p = 0.006), while inconsistent PPE use was significantly higher among those who received occupational health and safety (OHS) services (p = 0.034).Conclusion These findings emphasise the importance of PPE and occupational safety services to reduce eye injury risks in workplaces.

documents.abstract: The study examined the determinants of behavioral intention to use artificial intelligence (AI) among administrative personnel in selected private higher education institutions (HEIs) in Cebu, Philippines, using an extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) framework. The model incorporated trust in AI and AI job insecurity to provide a context-specific understanding of AI adoption in higher education administration. Using a quantitative, cross-sectional research design, data were collected from 243 administrative personnel and analyzed through structural equation modeling. The findings revealed that performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and social influence positively and significantly influenced behavioral intention, with social influence demonstrating the strongest relationship. Conversely, facilitating conditions and AI job insecurity did not significantly predict behavioral intention. Trust in AI exhibited a significant negative relationship with behavioral intention, contrary to the hypothesized positive direction. Multigroup analysis further indicated that gender significantly moderated the relationship between performance expectancy and behavioral intention, while institutional tenure moderated the relationship between social influence and behavioral intention. Age did not significantly moderate the relationship between effort expectancy and behavioral intention. The proposedTargeted Administrative Change Management framework provides a foundation for institutional strategies supporting responsible AI adoption, while its effectiveness warrants further empirical validation.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled data-science agents to automate multi-step analyses over heterogeneous files. However, incorrect choices regarding data sources, scope, or statistical definitions often lead to silent errors: computations execute successfully but produce plausible yet incorrect outputs that fail to answer the intended question. To mitigate this, we present RADAR, an auditable runtime that makes an agent's analytical choices inspectable and supports their revision through execution feedback. RADAR operates through three core mechanisms. First, an evidence-preserving exploration module retrieves task-relevant content while retaining source locations and observation coverage. Next, the runtime uses typed operators to record the agent's declared inputs, operation arguments, and resulting observations. Finally, runtime validation checks proposed operations against these observations. When a conflict is detected, the runtime rejects the operation or provides diagnostic feedback, allowing the agent to revise its choices before errors propagate. This design enables agents to fail loudly while leaving semantic interpretation to the LLM. On KramaBench, RADAR achieves overall scores of 0.723 with full source retrieval and 0.747 with gold sources supplied, corresponding to relative gains of 35.9% and 28.8% over the strongest baselines. Beyond KramaBench, RADAR achieves relative performance gains of 14.0% on DA-Code and 59.3% on DABStep, demonstrating its applicability across diverse agentic data-analysis workflows.

Multi-agent LLM systems are increasingly deployed in settings where individual agent failures can cascade across the collective, yet the mechanisms by which such failures propagate, and the structural conditions under which they are contained or corrected, remain poorly characterised. This paper synthesises seven findings from recent cs.MA and cs.DC preprints to argue a candidate structural pattern (a heuristic reading, not a derivation from a shared formal structure): systemic reliability in multi-agent LLM systems is not primarily a function of individual agent capability, but of the interaction between (a) the topology through which errors can propagate, (b) the credit-assignment mechanisms that identify which components generated the error, and (c) the architectural isolation boundaries that prevent a failure in one execution channel from contaminating others. We argue the analogy by naming specific mechanisms in each case rather than by appeal to a unified formalism. The corpus draws from cs.MA papers on multi-agent deliberation, self-evolution, coordination policy learning, and governance infrastructure, supplemented by cs.DC work on federated orchestration and zero-trust enforcement at physical actuation boundaries. Key findings include: deliberative consensus among LLM agents can degrade accuracy below single-model baselines when high-confidence wrong agents flip correct ones arXiv:2605.30802; architectural channel isolation failures silently block cross-agent memory injection regardless of agent-level correctness arXiv:2606.04896; governance layers at the execution boundary reduce unsafe executions from 88% to near-zero without modifying underlying generators arXiv:2606.04306; and temporal plus structural credit decomposition substantially reduces query complexity in MAS optimisation arXiv:2605.30227. Together these findings suggest that failure propagation and self-correction are topology-dependent phenomena that cannot be addressed by improving agent intelligence alone. Falsification path: if deliberative degradation disappears when inter-agent error correlation is experimentally reduced below 0.3, the error-propagation mechanism is confirmed; if it persists, the topology hypothesis is insufficient and capability variance must be the primary driver. Aim. This paper examines the role of family and faith community in strengthening psychosocial resilience, particularly among young people whose development is negatively affected by the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) and the prevailing context of post-truth culture. Concept. We proceed from the premise that the quality of family life and family resilience constitute key factors in the healthy intellectual, emotional, and psychosocial development of the individual. We reflect on the contemporary rise of mental health problems among young people within the post-truth context of a media-saturated environment, which emerges as a source of anxiety, weakened critical thinking, and the gradual erosion of emotional (EQ) and social intelligence (SQ). These parameters are projected in a dialectical relationship with the healthy faith community, which holds the potential to create a space of authentic intergenerational belonging, shared values, and social support. Results and Conclusion. The critical analysis develops an original argumentative framework, according to which high-quality family life, family resilience, and participation in healthy faith communities represent a significant dialectic of prevention against the psychosocial risks that current trends in AI use — within the context of post-truth culture — pose to the younger generation: rising anxiety, weakened psychosocial resilience, a limited capacity for deep relational bonds, and a diminished sense of meaning in life. Originality. The paper offers an original interdisciplinary synthesis at the intersection of family psychology, resilience studies, and the spirituality of the contemporary younger generation, providing an applicable model for counselling, pastoral, and educational practice.

Visual token reduction is an effective way to accelerate multimodal large language models (MLLMs), but performance deteriorates rapidly under extremely low token budgets. Existing work has explored both visual-token selection and training-based adaptation to reduced visual inputs. We take a step further by asking how a heavily compressed MLLM should learn from the states induced by its own generations. This setting naturally calls for on-policy self-distillation: a heavily compressed model is supervised on the states induced by its own generations, while its full-token counterpart serves as an information-rich teacher. Based on this insight, we propose LT-OPD, a training framework for extreme visual-token reduction. The student rolls out responses with only a small fraction of visual tokens, and a frozen full-token copy of the same MLLM provides distributional supervision along these student-generated trajectories. To stabilize on-policy learning when visual evidence is severely limited, we further introduce a budget-level curriculum that progressively decreases the token budget during training. Across nine benchmarks on Qwen3.5-4B, LT-OPD raises average retained performance under 5% visual-token retention from 68.6% to 82.3%, outperforming training-free, training-based, and reinforcement-learning baselines at the same budget. The gains transfer consistently to Qwen3.5-9B, GLM-4.6V-9B, and LLaVA-OV-1.5-4B. LT-OPD also reduces KV-cache usage by 85.2% and prefill FLOPs by 85.4% without additional inference overhead, demonstrating that on-policy learning can substantially recover capabilities lost to extreme visual-token reduction.

Public discourse about Artificial Intelligence (AI) relies on figurative language as a semiotic resource for conceptualising the technology. While previous research has examined metaphor and metonymy in such discourse, less attention has been paid to how these processes interact in shaping figurative construals of AI. Drawing on the Combined Input Hypothesis, this study analyses naturally occurring examples from published blogs and articles as instantiations of two broad types of figurative framings: those positioning the technology in relation to human activity and interaction, and those emerging from debates about its capabilities, risks, and limitations. The findings show that metonymy and metaphor perform distinct but complementary functions. Metonymy foregrounds contextually relevant aspects of AI, while metaphor organises these selected aspects into coherent interpretive configurations, shaping how the technology is construed in terms of its capabilities, relation to human agency, epistemic accessibility, and risks. This interaction gives rise to evaluations ranging from trust and collaboration to scepticism, awe, and fear. The study demonstrates the explanatory value of the Combined Input Hypothesis for understanding how metonymic profiling and metaphorical projection jointly structure figurative discourse about AI.

As AI agents are becoming widely adopted in the financial services industry, careful measurement is essential to understand where they can be reliably deployed and where oversight and professional review remain necessary. Such measurement, however, is constrained by limited access to proprietary or privacy-sensitive data. Existing benchmarks therefore often rely on publicly available data, human- and/or LLM-authored tasks, or simplified settings. We introduce FinancialAuditBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents on financial statement audit tasks, along with a framework for systematically generating synthetic engagements. Our task generation framework leverages differentially private aggregate statistics from historical audits along with audit expertise contributed through over 1,100 hours of benchmark development and review. FinancialAuditBench consists of 90 tasks spanning workpaper completion and review across six synthetic audit engagements, each containing an average of 179 files. Evaluation on eleven frontier models shows that while agents complete substantial portions of staff-level audit tasks well, they sometimes perform inappropriate procedures or produce incorrect documentation. Beyond financial auditing, our framework offers an approach for systematically generating synthetic tasks for model evaluation and training in privacy-sensitive domains.

documents.abstract: Monetary-policy announcements and central-bank communications play a central role in foreign exchange markets, yet their qualitative, unstructured form makes their forecasting value difficult to quantify. While prior research has largely focused on sentiment extracted from financial news, comparatively little is known about the relative contribution of different dimensions of monetary-policy communication. Existing studies primarily evaluate whether textual information improves overall forecasting performance but provide limited insight into which communication channels drive such improvements. To address this gap, this paper introduces a statistical attribution methodology that decomposes monetary-policy communication into interpretable channels and quantifies their incremental forecasting contribution under false-discovery-rate control. Monetary-policy news is transformed into structured communication signals using large language models (LLMs) and temporal feature engineering. These signals are evaluated using rolling-window experiments with tree-based machine-learning models. The results show that monetary-policy communication contains measurable predictive information. Attribution analysis shows that predictive value is concentrated in a small subset of signals, with communication timing providing the strongest individual feature-level contribution, targeted communication-activity measures also contributing positively, and LLM-derived sentiment providing complementary information at the group level. The findings indicate that communication-based forecasting value extends beyond sentiment alone and that attribution, rather than aggregate accuracy alone, is central to evaluating news-derived signals.
